subject: Chemistry
title: Chemical Bonding
learningOutcomes: Describe that noble gas electronic configuration and the octet and duplet rules help predict the chemical properties of main group elements.
Compare the formation of cations and anions.
Account for the electropositive nature of metals and the electronegative nature of non-metals.
Define ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.
Differentiate between ionic compounds and covalent compounds.
Explain the properties of compounds in terms of bonding and structure.
Compare the uses and properties of materials, such as strength and conductivity, as determined by the type of chemical bond between their atoms.
Interpret the strength of the forces of attraction and their effect on the melting and boiling points of ionic and covalent compounds.
Justify the availability of free charged particles (electrons or ions) for the conduction of electricity in ionic compounds, covalent compounds and metals.
Recognise that some substances ionise when dissolved in water, for example acids, which then conduct electricity.
Justify the use of graphite, diamond and metals for industrial purposes.
Draw the structure of ionic and covalent compounds along with their formation using dot-and-cross diagrams.

sections.heading: Why Atoms Form Bonds
sections.body: Atoms tend to decrease their energy by combining with other atoms, and this increases their stability. The noble gases show the pattern: helium has two electrons in its outermost shell and all the other noble gases have eight, so they neither combine with themselves nor with other atoms. Two electrons (duplet) or eight electrons (octet) in the outermost shell therefore mean stability. Sodium finds it easier to lose one electron than to gain seven, and hydrogen can lose an electron to become a proton or gain one to become a hydride ion. Alkali and alkaline earth metals are electropositive and bond with electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine.

sections.heading: Chemical Bond
sections.body: A chemical bond is a force of attraction that holds atoms together. When two atoms approach each other, attraction and repulsion both act. If attraction dominates, the energy of the system falls and a new molecule forms; if repulsion dominates, the atoms simply move apart. The chapter treats ionic, covalent and coordinate covalent bonds in section 3.2 and the metallic bond in section 3.3.

sections.heading: Ionic Bond
sections.body: An ionic bond forms by the complete transference of electron(s) from one atom to another so that both reach the configuration of the nearest noble gas. A sodium atom (2, 8, 1) gives its outer electron to a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7), giving Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that attract each other by an electrostatic force. Calcium loses two electrons and combines with two chlorine atoms to form CaCl₂. The ions surround each other three-dimensionally in a crystal lattice. A metal usually reacts with a non-metal to form an ionic bond, and only outermost-shell electrons take part.

sections.heading: Covalent Bond
sections.body: A covalent bond forms by the mutual sharing of electrons so that each atom acquires the configuration of the nearest noble gas. As two atoms approach, attraction and repulsion act together, and at the distance where attraction dominates, the total energy is minimum and a stable molecule forms. A bond can be single (H₂, Cl₂, H₂O, CH₄), double (O₂, CO₂, C₂H₄) or triple (N₂, HCN). A bond between two identical atoms is non-polar; a bond between two non-identical atoms is polar, with partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻ and the shared pair bent towards the more electronegative atom.

sections.heading: Coordinate Covalent Bond
sections.body: In a coordinate covalent bond the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only. The donor has a lone pair and the acceptor has an empty or partially empty outer shell. A proton accepts a lone pair of water to form the hydroxonium ion H₃O⁺, ammonia gives a pair to H⁺ to form the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ (as in NH₄Cl), and NH₃ gives a pair to boron of BF₃ (H₃N → BF₃). The bond is shown by an arrow head pointing towards the acceptor. Once formed it is exactly like a covalent bond, and when it breaks, both electrons go to the donor.

sections.heading: Metallic Bond
sections.body: Metals have low ionisation energy, so their atoms lose outer electrons easily. In sodium metal each atom is surrounded by eight others, and the outer electrons move freely among them. No electron stays on one nucleus, so a metal has a sea of electrons in which all the positive ions are submerged. The metallic bond is the attraction between the positive ions and the mobile electrons. Its strength depends on the number of positive charges on the ions and the number of mobile electrons set free by each atom, so magnesium (two electrons per atom) has a stronger bond than sodium.

sections.heading: Electropositive Character of Metals
sections.body: Metals tend to lose electrons and form cations; this is their electropositive character, and it is related to reactivity. Alkali metals (Na, K) are highly electropositive; they react vigorously with water and halogens to give hydroxides and halides and with acids to give salts and hydrogen. Alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca) lose electrons less easily and react less vigorously. Aluminium is also highly electropositive and reacts readily with mineral acids.

sections.heading: Electronegative Character of Non-metals
sections.body: Non-metals have an affinity for electrons and form anions, so they are called electronegative elements. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, followed by oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine. Non-metals react with metals to form ionic bonds and with other non-metals to form a wide variety of molecular substances.

sections.heading: Ionic and Covalent Compounds Compared
sections.body: Ionic compounds are crystalline solids of oppositely charged ions with high melting and boiling points; NaCl melts at 801 °C. They are generally soluble in polar solvents such as water and conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution because of free ions. Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules made of two or more non-metals. Those of low molecular mass are gases or low-boiling liquids and those of high molecular mass are solids. They generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors.

sections.heading: Intermolecular Forces
sections.body: Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are generally very weak compared with bonds between atoms. They are weakest among gas molecules and strongest among solid molecules, and the stronger they are, the higher the melting and boiling points. Dipole–dipole forces act between molecules of a polar compound such as HCl, where the δ⁺ end of one molecule attracts the δ⁻ end of the next. Hydrogen bonding is a special case of dipole–dipole attraction that occurs when hydrogen is bonded to F, O or N, as in water, which is why water has higher melting and boiling points than H₂S and NH₃.

sections.heading: Nature of Bonding and Properties
sections.body: Ionic bonds are non-directional because the ions are spherical, and the lattice breaks easily under force, so ionic solids are brittle. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct because the ions are tightly held, but molten or dissolved ones do. Water hydrates the free ions, and ions in solution can react, as Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ give a white precipitate of AgCl. Diamond has each carbon bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds, so it is the hardest thing on the planet and is used for cutting, polishing and drilling. Graphite has layers that slip and mobile electrons between them, so it is a lubricant and an electrode. Metals are drawn into wires and sheets because their rows of atoms slip over one another. HCl, H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ ionise completely in water.

definitions.definition: A force of attraction between atoms that holds them together.
The arrangement of electrons around the nucleus in shells and sub-shells.
Two electrons in the outermost (first) shell mean stability, as in H and He.
Eight electrons in the outermost shell mean stability, as in the noble gases other than helium.
An atom or group of atoms that carries a positive or negative charge.
A positive ion formed when an atom loses electron(s).
A negative ion formed when an atom gains electron(s).
A bond formed by the complete transference of electron(s) from one atom to another; also called an electrovalent bond.
The three-dimensional arrangement in which oppositely charged ions surround each other.
A bond formed by the mutual sharing of electrons between atoms.
A covalent bond with one, two or three shared electron pairs.
A covalent bond between two non-identical atoms with partial charges δ⁺ and δ⁻.
A covalent bond between two identical atoms; the shared pair lies in the middle.
A covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only.
The donor provides the electron pair; the acceptor has an empty or partially empty outer shell.
H₃O⁺, formed when a proton bonds to the oxygen of a water molecule.
A bond in which positively charged ions are bound together by mobile electrons.
The mobile outer electrons that move freely among the positive ions in a metal.
The tendency of metals to lose electrons and form cations.
The affinity of non-metals for electrons; they form anions.
Weak forces of attraction between the molecules of elements and compounds.
Attraction between the δ⁺ end of one polar molecule and the δ⁻ end of the next.
A special case of dipole–dipole attraction when hydrogen is bonded to F, O or N.
The surrounding and interaction of ions or molecules by water molecules.
Breaking easily under an external force, as ionic solids do.
Having no regular crystalline form, as coal does.
The splitting of a covalent molecule such as HCl into ions when it dissolves in water.

examTips: Duplet = 2 electrons (H, He); octet = 8 electrons (all other noble gases). Atoms bond to reach these stable arrangements.
Ionic bond: transfer of electron(s), metal to non-metal, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻ type ions in a crystal lattice. Covalent bond: sharing of electrons between non-metals.
Single bond = one shared pair (—), double = two (=), triple = three (≡). O₂ is double, N₂ is triple, H₂ and Cl₂ are single.
Polar bond = two non-identical atoms (HCl, H₂O); non-polar bond = two identical atoms (H₂, Cl₂). The more electronegative atom gets δ⁻.
Coordinate bond: both electrons come from the donor (lone pair) and go to the acceptor (empty orbital); shown by an arrow towards the acceptor (H₃N → BF₃, H₃O⁺, NH₄⁺).
Metallic bond strength depends on the charge of the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons per atom: Mg (2 electrons) is stronger than Na (1 electron).
Fluorine is the most electronegative element, followed by oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine. Alkali metals are more electropositive than alkaline earth metals.

Ionic solids: high melting point (NaCl 801 °C), brittle, soluble in water, conduct only when molten or dissolved. Covalent compounds: low melting points, bad conductors, usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
Intermolecular forces are weakest in gases and strongest in solids. Hydrogen bonding (H on F, O or N) explains why water is a liquid while H₂S is a gas.

Link the property to the bonding: diamond is hard (rigid covalent network), graphite is slippery and conducts (layers and mobile electrons), metals are ductile and conduct (rows slip, sea of electrons).

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many electrons are present in the outermost shell of helium?

options: Eight
Four
Two
One

practiceQuestions.explanation: Helium has two electrons in its outermost shell (the duplet); all the other noble gases have eight.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which bond is formed by the complete transference of electron(s) from one atom to another?

options: Covalent bond
Ionic bond
Coordinate covalent bond
Metallic bond

practiceQuestions.explanation: An ionic bond forms by the complete transference of electron(s) from one atom to another.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which element is the most electronegative in the periodic table?

options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Chlorine
Fluorine

practiceQuestions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, followed by oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which molecule contains a triple covalent bond?

options: N₂
O₂
H₂
Cl₂

practiceQuestions.explanation: Nitrogen (N₂) has a triple bond; O₂ has a double bond and H₂ and Cl₂ have single bonds.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In the hydroxonium ion H₃O⁺, which particle donates the electron pair to the proton?

options: A hydrogen atom of the water molecule
The oxygen atom of the water molecule
The proton itself
Both hydrogen atoms equally

practiceQuestions.explanation: The oxygen atom of water has lone pairs; it donates one pair to the proton (acceptor) to form a coordinate covalent bond.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why is graphite used as an industrial lubricant?

options: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds
It is the hardest substance on the planet
Its layers are not strongly bonded and slip past each other
Its ions move freely in the solid

practiceQuestions.explanation: Graphite has layers of hexagonal rings that are not strongly bonded and slip past one another.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why do solid ionic compounds not conduct electricity?

options: Their ions are tightly held and cannot move
They contain no ions
They contain mobile electrons that are blocked
They are made of discrete molecules

practiceQuestions.explanation: In the solid state the ions are held in the crystal lattice and cannot move; they conduct only when molten or dissolved.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The metallic bond in magnesium is stronger than in sodium. Which reason is correct?

options: Each Na atom sets free two mobile electrons and forms a 2+ ion
Each Mg atom sets free two mobile electrons and forms a 2+ ion, while each Na atom sets free one and forms a 1+ ion
Magnesium atoms have no mobile electrons
Sodium ions carry a higher positive charge than magnesium ions

practiceQuestions.explanation: Bond strength depends on the charge of the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons per atom; Mg has more of both.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A hydrogen atom can gain one electron to form a hydride ion and complete its duplet.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hydrogen can lose one electron to become H⁺ or gain one to become the hydride ion H⁻, which completes its duplet.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Covalent compounds are usually good conductors of electricity.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Covalent compounds are usually bad conductors of electricity.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Ionic bonds are directional because the ions are spherical.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The ions are spherical and surround each other from all sides, so ionic bonds are non-directional.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Intermolecular forces are weakest among the molecules of a gas.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Intermolecular forces are weakest among gas molecules and strongest among solid molecules.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only is called a ____ covalent bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a coordinate covalent bond one atom, the donor, provides both electrons of the shared pair.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The surrounding of ions by water molecules is called ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hydration means water molecules surround and interact with ions or molecules.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The attraction between positive ions and mobile electrons in a metal is called the ____ bond.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A metallic bond holds positively charged ions together by mobile electrons.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the steps in the formation of sodium chloride in the correct order.

items: The oppositely charged ions attract each other by electrostatic force
A sodium atom (2, 8, 1) loses its outermost electron
The ions surround each other three-dimensionally in a crystal lattice
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are formed, each with a noble gas configuration
The electron is accepted by a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7)
correctOrder: A sodium atom (2, 8, 1) loses its outermost electron
The electron is accepted by a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7)
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are formed, each with a noble gas configuration
The oppositely charged ions attract each other by electrostatic force
The ions surround each other three-dimensionally in a crystal lattice

sequencingActivity.explanation: Sodium loses its outer electron, chlorine accepts it, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ form with noble gas configurations, the ions attract each other and then pack into a crystal lattice.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: NaCl melts at 801 °C, while HCl is a gas at room temperature. Which explanation is correct?

options: NaCl consists of discrete molecules with weak forces, while HCl has a crystal lattice of ions
Both have the same type of forces, but NaCl is heavier
NaCl has strong electrostatic forces between its ions, which are hard to break, while HCl has discrete molecules held by weak intermolecular forces
HCl has strong ionic bonds between its molecules, while NaCl has none

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Ionic compounds have strong electrostatic forces in a crystal lattice and therefore high melting points; covalent compounds such as HCl exist as molecules with weak forces between them.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A solid conducts electricity, can be drawn into wires and contains no ions. What does its structure contain?

options: Oppositely charged ions in a rigid crystal lattice
Positive ions surrounded by a sea of mobile electrons
Discrete neutral molecules with no free particles
Layers of ions held by hydrogen bonds

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: These are the properties of a metal: mobile electrons conduct, and rows of atoms slip over one another so it can be drawn into wires.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Ammonia donates its lone pair to the boron atom of BF₃. Which statement is correct?

options: A coordinate covalent bond forms, with B as the donor, shown as H₃N ← BF₃
An ionic bond forms because N loses electrons to B
A metallic bond forms between N and B
A coordinate covalent bond forms, with N as the donor and B as the acceptor, shown as H₃N → BF₃

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: The arrow points from the donor (N, which has the lone pair) to the acceptor (B, which has an empty outer shell).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why is H₂O a liquid while H₂S is a gas at room temperature?

options: Water is polar and strong hydrogen bonding exists between its molecules
The water molecule is lighter than the H₂S molecule
Oxygen has a larger atomic size than sulphur
H₂S has strong hydrogen bonding but water has none

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Hydrogen bonded to oxygen gives highly polar O–H bonds, so strong attraction exists between water molecules; this gives water higher melting and boiling points.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Which set of changes correctly describes the formation of calcium chloride from calcium and chlorine atoms?

options: Ca → Ca⁺ + e⁻ and Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻
Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ and 2Cl + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻
Ca + 2e⁻ → Ca²⁻ and 2Cl → 2Cl⁺ + 2e⁻
Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cl + 2e⁻ → Cl²⁻

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Calcium loses two electrons to form Ca²⁺ and each of two chlorine atoms gains one electron to form Cl⁻, giving CaCl₂.
